extracted.intended_audience: immigration applicants, petitioners, attorneys, petition preparers, and stakeholders responding to or affected by the DHS proposed public-charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the proposed regulatory requirements, documentation, time-burden assumptions, fee rules, and procedural steps (RFEs, bonds, appeals) that DHS would impose under the 2018 public-charge proposed rule for Forms I-485, I-944, I-129, I-129CW, I-539, and related forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to submit Form I-944 for adjustment of status
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would create Form I-944 to collect information so USCIS could determine whether an applicant would be inadmissible based on public charge grounds; the proposed rule would require individuals who are applying for adjustment of status to complete and submit the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form I-944 would collect information based on factors such as age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills. DHS assumes that all individuals who apply for adjustment of status using Form I-485 are required to submit Form I-944, unless the individual is in a class of applicants that is exempt from review for determination of inadmissibility based on public charge at the time of adjustment of status according to statute or regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary RFE issuance to require Form I-944 for some nonimmigrant filings
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS officers would be able to exercise discretion regarding whether it would be necessary to issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) requiring submission of Form I-944 for Form I-129, Form I-129CW beneficiaries, and Form I-539 applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all nonimmigrants who apply for extension of stay or change of status would be required to file Form I-944. DHS is unable to estimate how many RFEs adjudicators may issue since issuance would be discretionary; for cost-range analysis DHS presents RFE rates of 10 to 100 percent to show possible impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required submission of credit report and credit score with Form I-944
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must bear the cost of obtaining a credit report and credit score from any one of the three major credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) to be submitted with the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS does not assume applicants can obtain a free credit report specifically for filing Form I-944 and thus assumes each applicant would obtain a credit report and credit score from at least one bureau. DHS estimates the cost at $19.95 per applicant (based on prices from major bureaus) and included this cost in annualized estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-burden estimate for completing Form I-944 (4.5 hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates the time burden associated with filing Form I-944 is 4 hours and 30 minutes (4.5 hours) per applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The time burden includes reviewing instructions, gathering required documentation and information, completing the declaration, preparing statements, attaching necessary documentation, and submitting the declaration. DHS calculates opportunity cost of time for Form I-944 using the minimum wage rate of $10.66 per hour, yielding an estimated $47.97 per applicant and annualized totals using population estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased Form I-485 time burden (+10 minutes) and associated costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would add additional instructions to Form I-485, increasing the estimated time to complete the form by 10 minutes (from 6.25 hours to 6.42 hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time burden includes reading instructions, gathering documents, completing the application, preparing statements, attaching documentation, and submitting. DHS uses a $10.66/hour rate (minimum wage) to compute opportunity cost; DHS estimates the proposed increase yields additional annual costs ($691,898) compared to baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased time burdens for petition/extension forms (+30 minutes each)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would require additional information/instructions on Forms I-129, I-129CW, and I-539, increasing the time to complete each form by 30 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provides current and proposed time estimates and associated opportunity costs: Form I-129 current 2.34 hours → proposed 2.84 hours; Form I-129CW current 3.0 hours → proposed 3.5 hours; Form I-539 current 1.88 hours → proposed 2.38 hours. DHS uses an average total compensation rate of $35.78/hour for petitioners to compute per-petitioner opportunity costs and multiplies by estimated annual filing populations to estimate aggregate impacts (including calculated new costs for each form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond process and associated form requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: At DHS's discretion, certain aliens found likely to become a public charge may be provided the opportunity to post a public charge bond; an obligor would submit the bond using Form I-945, and cancellation would use Form I-356.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If cancellation of a bond is denied, DHS would notify the obligor and inform them of the possibility to appeal to the USCIS Administrative Appeals Office (AAO) using Form I-290B. Upon learning of a breach of a public charge bond, DHS would notify the obligor that the bond has been declared breached and inform the obligor of the possibility to appeal the determination to the AAO using Form I-290B. DHS provides estimated filing fees and opportunity cost assumptions for these forms in its cost table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to submit Form I-407 upon certain departure/loss of LPR status
rubrics_metrics.description: If the alien permanently departed the United States as defined in proposed 8 CFR 213.1, and the loss of LPR status was voluntary, DHS would require a Form I-407 submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This submission is tied to the public charge/bond processes and the rule's definitions of permanent departure; DHS notes this as part of the procedural steps under the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specified wage rates and methodology for opportunity cost calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS calculates opportunity cost of time using specified hourly rates depending on the filing population: $10.66/hour (minimum wage) for many applicants (e.g., I-944/I-485) and $35.78/hour (average total compensation) for petitioners (e.g., I-129 series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS multiplies time-burden hours by the assigned wage rate to compute per-applicant opportunity cost, and then multiplies by estimated annual population filings to arrive at annual opportunity-cost estimates. The document shows detailed calculations and rounded totals for each form and for proposed vs. current scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing fee and biometrics fee rules for Forms (fee amounts and exemptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The document states the current filing fee for Form I-539 is $370 and notes certain classes (A and G nonimmigrants) are not required to pay that fee; a biometrics services fee of $85 is required for V nonimmigrants and certain CNMI applicants for initial nonimmigrant status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS indicates some fees are set to recover processing costs. The economic analysis multiplies filing fees by estimated annual populations to compute aggregate filing-fee costs. The proposed rule would also add or assume other fees for new forms (e.g., Form I-945 bond fees shown in the cost table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of information collected on Form I-944 (public-charge factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form I-944 would collect information based on factors such as age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills so USCIS could determine likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerated set of factors forms the substantive basis for public-charge determinations under the proposed rule and explains why applicants must assemble documentation (credit reports, evidence of assets/resources, health information, education/skills documentation) as part of the filing and why time burdens and costs increase.
